15.2 Quadrant A: Acquisition Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

The first quadrant of the Brand Axis includes consumers who are typically unaware of the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to environmental distractions.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by uncertain environmental conditions, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by uncertain environmental conditions.  Likewise, consumers closest to the Y-axis are conceptually more aware than those further away from the same axis.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as an acquisition strategy to focus more heavily on ascertaining new customers that never have, or very rarely, purchased their product or service previously.  However, in this particular quadrant, these consumers are not distracted by competitive offerings but are uncertain of the product due to environmental constraints.  These environmental constraints can include socio-economic, political/regulatory, cultural, or technological forces that prohibit consumers from purchasing.  Whether the reason includes not having enough money, not having the technological ability, not having a cultural significance, or not having access to the product or service, consumers in this quadrant do not know that the product or service is even available.  This lack of awareness keeps them outside of the targeted audience of the balanced message magnet centered over the direct middle of the Brand Axis.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware and too focused on accessing these consumers at the expense of their entire branding message.  This is known as a misaligned push scenario, which is due to a company’s (or individual’s) own internal strategic decisions.  In these “push” cases, a hyper-focus on a quadrant of consumers can cause a company to become misaligned, moving the message magnet from the center of the Brand Axis into the focused quadrant.  [Note, a market share growth into this quadrant is possible with a balanced message over time, meaning that the size of the message magnet can grow and expand further into this quadrant, but a misaligned move into this quadrant often comes in haste, trying to capture these potential customers without a balanced campaign.]  A rush to capture more consumers in the quadrant causes the message magnet to become off-brand, causing the current message magnet not to grow but to move off-center.  As it moves into this quadrant, less of the message magnet becomes equally shared by the other three quadrants.

For example, in the scenario above, you can see that the internal decisions of this firm have pushed the message magnet off-center.  The push structure is indicated by the hub, which is typically in the center of the message magnet where the brand and the brand spokes consist, which has moved closer to the edge of the message magnet border, insinuating that it is pushing the entire message magnet off-center. This means that this misaligned push approach has increased Quadrant A from a balanced approach of 25% to an unbalanced level of 70% of the marketing message. In this case, the other quadrants, which when balanced would all be equal to 25% of the message, have become disproportionate, decreasing to 12%, 4%, and 14%, respectively across the other quadrants.

The previous discussion focused on the internal decisions that cause companies (or individuals) to push the message magnet into misalignment inadvertently.  In another realistic scenario, companies can also be pulled by environmental factors into the same position.  As you can see in the example above, the percentages of targeted customers from each quadrant stay the same. Still, the hub has moved into the bottom right of the message magnet, demonstrating that it is being pulled in the direction of Quadrant A.  This is known as a misaligned pull scenario, which is due to external forces acting on a company or individual, causing them to move off the center of the Brand Axis.  Here, the hub of the magnet is trying to stay on center due to marketing messages that attempt to stay on brand; however, external forces are naturally pulling the company or individual message in that direction away from the centered position on the brand axis.

In this quadrant, these external forces can be the same environmental forces that are making consumers unaware that the brand exists, and even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address this environmental uncertainty to acquire new customers, there in some cases may be no way to avoid it.   This is not atypical of regulatory and technological changes in the environment.  When major laws are passed, like the Patriot Act, some industries are pulled into a particular stance with their messaging.  While they may not want to address or discuss these issues within their marketing space to gain new customers, they may have no choice but to address these new policy issues, which could naturally pull them off the center of the Brand Axis.  While this external scenario may not be as prevalent as the internal one in this quadrant, it can happen in certain industries.

The Impacts

As highlighted in the percentage numbers in the graphics above, the impact of this quadrant becomes overly focused on new customers.  While a company either intentionally (internal push misalignment) or unintentionally (external pull misalignment) moves into this quadrant due to environmental uncertainty, loyal customers are slipping out the back door.  This misalignment creates major inefficiencies due to the decreased impact of returning customers.  As you can tell from the percentages below, only 16% of the marketing message is now organically directed at returning customers, which is a decrease of 34%.  Hypothetically speaking, if a company or individual were to lose 34% of the existing or returning revenue, there most likely would be an immense amount of revenue loss.  However, this scenario occurs every day as firms become overly aggressive to move into new markets.  It can sometimes occur even when trying to stay balanced but are pulled into this quadrant due to changing environmental conditions.
title: 15.2 Quadrant A: Acquisition Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

15.3 Quadrant B: Retention Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

The second quadrant of the Brand Axis includes consumers who have typically forgotten about the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to environmental distractions.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by uncertain environmental conditions, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by uncertain environmental conditions.  Likewise, consumers further away from Y-axis are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as a retention strategy to focus more heavily on retaining loyal customers that have frequently purchased their product or service previously but are beginning to forget about the product or service.  However, in this particular quadrant, these consumers are not distracted by competitive offerings but are uncertain of the product due to environmental constraints.  As previously discussed, these environmental constraints can include socio-economic, political/regulatory, cultural, or technological forces that prohibit a consumer from repurchasing.  Whether the reason includes a reduction in income, cultural relevance, technological know-how, or the recent inability to access the product or service, consumers in this quadrant are moving away from purchasing this brand, even though they may have purchased in the past.  This extinction of the brand in the consumer's mind has made them no longer a target audience of the balanced message magnet but into space beyond the magnet’s border.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware of their previous consumers’ movement away from the brand and become overly focused on retaining these customers at the expense of their entire branding message.  Again, this misaligned push scenario results from an internal decision to recapture these consumers while reducing the balanced attention on acquiring new customers at the same time. For example, in the scenario below, you can see that the internal decisions of this firm have pushed the message magnet off-center. In this quadrant, the message magnet becomes unbalanced, causing the company to move 70% of its messaging focus into this quadrant and away from the other three quadrants. In this case, the other quadrants have decreased to 14%, 4%, and 12%, respectively, across the other quadrants.  This means that this misaligned push approach in Quadrant B has increased from a balanced 25% to an unbalanced level of 70% of the marketing message.

As discussed in the previous section, the same is true for Quadrant B; that is, a firm can be “pulled” into magnetic misalignment as well.  In this quadrant, it again is the same environmental forces that are making consumers forget that the brand exists, and even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address this environmental uncertainty to acquire new customers, there in some cases, again, might be no way to avoid it.   Just like in Quadrant A, this is not atypical for regulatory and technological changes in the environment.  For example, when 5G becomes the cellular network norm, some companies may get stymied in their marketing message due to this technological advancement.  Customers may switch brands due to use innovativeness and how they utilize apps on their devices.  In this quadrant, some industries may be pulled into a particular stance with their messaging.  While they may not want to address or discuss these issues within their marketing space, to retain customers, they may have no choice but to address these new technological advances, even to the extent of not focusing on the balance of new customers, which could naturally pull them off the center of the Brand Axis, as indicated in the figure below.

The Impacts

As highlighted in the percentage numbers in the graphics above, the impact of this quadrant becomes overly focused on previous customers.  While a company either intentionally (internal push misalignment) or unintentionally (external pull misalignment) moves into this quadrant due to environmental uncertainty, opportunities in appealing to new customers are missed.  This misalignment creates additional inefficiencies due to the decreased impact of new customers.  As you can tell from the percentages above, only 16% of the marketing message is now organically directed at new customers, which is a decrease of 34%.  Hypothetically speaking, if a company or individual were to lose 34% of potential new revenue, there most likely would be an immense amount of revenue loss because the same return is unlikely in retaining the old customers who are moving on from your brand due to environmental disruptions.  However, this scenario occurs every day as firms become overly aggressive to retain old customers moving away from the brand.  It can even occur when they are trying to stay balanced but are pulled into this quadrant due to changing environmental conditions.
title: 15.3 Quadrant B: Retention Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

15.4 Quadrant C: Retention Focus within Competitive Intensity

The third quadrant of the Brand Axis includes consumers who have typically forgotten about the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to competitive intensity.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers positioned closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by competitive messages, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by competitors.  Likewise, consumers further away from Y-axis are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as a retention strategy to focus more heavily on retaining loyal customers.  These consumers have previously purchased their product or service but are beginning to forget about the brand due to other attractive, more competitive options.  For many possible different reasons, these competitors are gaining the appeal of the target consumers away from their previous brand.  In most instances, the value equation of the company’s (or individual’s) brand has been diminished due to a decrease in the perception of one or more of the four P’s: Product, Place, Price, or Promotion.  [Note: A decrease in the perception of price is actually a price increase.]  This forgetting of the brand in the consumer's mind has moved them outside the borders of a balanced message magnet, as the consumer is no longer part of the company’s (or individual’s) target market.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware of their previous consumers’ movement away from the brand and become overly focused on retaining these customers at the expense of their entire branding message.  Again, this misaligned push scenario results from an internal decision to recapture these consumers while reducing the balanced attention on acquiring new customers at the same time.  As highlighted in the example below, the message magnet becomes unbalanced, causing the company to move 70% of its messaging focus into this quadrant and away from the other three quadrants.  As you can ascertain, the internal decisions of this firm have pushed the message magnet off-center.  In this case, the other quadrants have decreased to 14%, 4%, and 12%, respectively, across the other quadrants.  This means that this misaligned push approach in Quadrant C has increased from a balanced 25% to an unbalanced level of 70% of the marketing message.

As discussed in previous sections, Quadrant C is similar in that a firm can be “pulled” into magnetic misalignment.  In this quadrant, the same competitive forces that make consumers forget that the brand exists are causing the brand to become misaligned.  Even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address these exact competitors’ attempts to steal market share, competitive advertising may thrust the company (or individual) into the heat of the battle.  In fact, for this very reason, some countries do not allow competitive advertising.  Like in South Africa, the practice is considered illegal, although, in the United States, we see it all of the time (e.g., Ford vs. Chevy Trucks).  In this example, some companies (or individuals) can be pulled into misalignment by the actions of competing firms, which could naturally pull them off the center of the Brand Axis, as indicated in the figure below.

The Impacts

As highlighted in the percentage numbers in the graphics above, the impact of this quadrant becomes overly focused on retaining previous customers at the expense of acquiring new ones.  While a company either intentionally (internal push misalignment) or unintentionally (external pull misalignment) moves into this quadrant due to competitive intensity, opportunities in appealing to new customers are overlooked.  As in Quadrant B, this misalignment creates inefficiencies due to the decreased impact of new customers.  As demonstrated from the percentages above, only 16% of the marketing message is now organically directed at new customers, a decrease of 34%.  Hypothetically speaking, if a company or individual were to lose 34% of potential new revenue, there most likely would be an immense amount of profit loss because the same return is unlikely in retaining the old customers who are moving on from your brand due to competitive intensity.  As with all other quadrants, the misalignment creates unequaled opportunity, resulting in fewer sales and lost profit.  Although, this scenario occurs every day as firms become overly aggressive to retain old customers moving away from the brand.  It occurs even when they are trying to stay balanced but are pulled into this quadrant due to competition.
title: 15.4 Quadrant C: Retention Focus within Competitive Intensity

15.5 Quadrant D: Acquisition Focus within Competitive Intensity

The fourth and final quadrant consumers are typically unaware of the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to competitive intensity.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers positioned closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by competitive messages, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by competitors.  Likewise, consumers further away from Y-axis are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Likewise, consumers closest to the Y-axis are conceptually more aware of the brand than those further away from the same axis.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as an acquisition strategy to focus more heavily on establishing new customers.  These consumers have never, or very rarely, purchased the brand previously due to having already been persuaded by other competing brands.  For many possible different reasons, these competitors have already gained the appeal of the target consumers before the customer might even consider the company’s (or individual’s) brand.  In most instances, the value equation of the competing brand has already convinced consumers towards their brand due to a competitive advantage across one or more of the four P’s: Product, Place, Price, or Promotion.  The unawareness of the company’s (or individual’s) brand in the consumer's mind has prevented them from entering into the borders of a balanced message magnet, as the consumer has never previously become part of the company’s (or individual’s) target market.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware and too focused on accessing these consumers at the expense of their entire branding message.  Again, this misaligned push scenario results from an internal decision to capture these consumers while reducing the balanced attention on retaining new customers at the same time.  As demonstrated in the example below, the message magnet becomes unbalanced, causing the company to move 70% of its messaging focus into this quadrant and away from the other three quadrants.  As you can see, the internal decisions of this firm have pushed the message magnet off-center.  In this case, the other quadrants have decreased to 12%, 4%, and 14%, respectively, across the other quadrants.  This means that this misaligned push approach in Quadrant D has increased from a balanced 25% to an unbalanced level of 70% of the marketing message.

As discussed in previous sections, Quadrant D is similar in that a firm can also experience a misaligned pull scenario.  In this quadrant, the same competitive forces that are making consumers unaware that the company’s (or individual’s) brand exists are causing the brand to become misaligned.  Even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address these exact competitors’ attempt to allow any consideration of another brand, the saturation of a competitor’s message within the overall market may demand that the company (or individual) address their own competitive disadvantages in the marketplace. In this example, the company (or individual) can be pulled into misalignment by the mere marketing actions of competing firms, which would force them to move towards consumers that may have never heard of their brand, or at least, very little about the brand.  In this example, the sheer lack of market share due to the competitive dominance of other brands can move the message magnet off-center of the Brand Axis, as indicated in the figure below.

The Impacts

As highlighted in the percentage numbers in the graphics above, the impact of this quadrant becomes overly focused on acquiring new customers at the expense of retaining previous ones.  While a company either intentionally (internal push misalignment) or unintentionally (external pull misalignment) moves into this quadrant due to competitive intensity, opportunities in keeping prior customers are being overlooked.  Just like in Quadrant A, this misalignment creates inefficiencies due to the decreased impact of previous customers.  As demonstrated from the percentages above, only 16% of the marketing message is now organically directed at loyal customers, a decrease of 34%.  Hypothetically speaking, if a company or individual were to lose 34% of potential new revenue, there most likely would be an immense amount of profit loss because the same return is unlikely in acquiring new customers who have never heard of the brand due to competitive intensity.  As with all other quadrants, the misalignment creates unequaled opportunity, resulting in fewer sales and lost profit.  Although this scenario occurs every day as firms become overly aggressive to acquire new customers at the expense of their competitors, they are just being pulled into this quadrant due to competition intensity.
title: 15.5 Quadrant D: Acquisition Focus within Competitive Intensity
